newsitem.title: THAILAND: CSCE woos Thai sugar industry interest in futures.
newsitem.headline: CSCE woos Thai sugar industry interest in futures.

text.p: The New York-based Coffee, Sugar & Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) on Monday urged the Thai sugar industry, one of the biggest in the world, to trade more options and recently-introduced white sugar contracts at the exchange.

"We think (the white sugar contracts) would be very interesting to the Thai sugar industry because it is a 100 ICUMSA which (Thailand) produces a lot..." CSCE president James Bowe told Reuters in an interview.
"Moreover, we are very flexible in terms of delivery. We think (the market) will create effective hedging mechanisms over a long term," he said.

Thailand is expected to export around 4.5 million tonnes of sugar for the 1996/97 crop year. The majority of Thai sugar exports pricing is based on the New York number 11 contract which is the world raw sugar contract.
Moreover, most Thai mills also hedge at the CSCE futures market through international trading houses.

But Thai sugar exporters, producers and traders barely used options to manage their risks due to lack of market knowledge on the instruments or traded in the 100 ICUMSA market introduced in June last year.
The CSCE white sugar contracts specified that the product must be white sugar of 100 ICUMSA in polypropylene bags which must be delivered at 84 ports in 38 countries.
He said it would be more convenient and cheaper to trade the white contracts at the New York CSCE.
"The trade is available in the same New York 11 pit. You can actually trade the white premiums in one transaction, just like doing a spread trade between the two markets," he said.
Although Bowe described the present white contracts trading volume as "negligible", he expected the activities to pick up.
"In new markets no one wants to go first, if you are wrong it is terrible...But the market will pick up once the industry recognises its utility," he said.
On options, Bowe said the instrument would offer Thai sugar industry new opportunities to create trading depth.
He said the equal access to information made it less attractive to limit sugar risk management only to futures trading.

Bowe said despite the size of the industry in Thailand, it was not feasible to create a competitive futures markets to CSCE contracts here or elsewhere in Asia or expand trading hours due to doubts about liquidity.
"Our experience to date has been there is not enough economic sense to have competing markets...because the market is only successful if it is liquid," he said.
